question: Are NYC's streets more dangerous at night? Make a chart and give a conclusion for a news report.

options.metric: Average number of police-reported crashes per clock-hour slot per calendar day
options.denominator: Sum of calendar days in 2013–2025 multiplied by 14 daytime clock-hour slots (06:00–19:59) or 10 nighttime clock-hour slots (20:00–05:59)
options.reason: Normalizing crash counts by the number of clock-hour slots makes the unequal lengths of the daytime and nighttime periods comparable.
options.answer: This dataset can only partly answer the question because it has no traffic-exposure denominator; in complete years 2013–2025 it records 24.18 daytime crashes versus 10.55 nighttime crashes per calendar-day clock-hour slot.
options.interpretation: This is only a partial answer: the chart measures one row per NYC police-reported crash as average crashes per clock-hour slot per calendar day across complete calendar years 2013–2025, with daytime defined as 06:00–19:59 and nighttime as 20:00–05:59, and shows 24.18 by day versus 10.55 by night. This is a defensible comparison of reported crash frequency because its denominator accounts for 14 daytime versus 10 nighttime clock-hour slots on each calendar day. It leaves unanswered whether risk per trip or mile differs because the file has no traffic-exposure measure. Checks found no missing dates or times (and the typed DATE/TIME columns rule out string or impossible values); 23,787 of 2,132,218 full-year dated crashes at 00:00 were excluded as potentially default times, and partial years 2012 (100,545 crashes) and 2026 (36,424) were excluded.

options.metric: Crashes with at least one person injured as a share of crashes with a known number_of_persons_injured
options.denominator: Crashes in each time period with a nonmissing number_of_persons_injured
options.reason: The share of crashes involving injury compares crash-level harm while avoiding the different numbers of crashes occurring in each time period.
options.answer: This dataset can only partly answer the question because it lacks traffic-exposure data; 28.33% of nighttime crashes involved an injury, compared with 23.33% of daytime crashes.
options.interpretation: This is only a partial answer: the chart shows, for one row per NYC police-reported crash in complete years 2013–2025, the share with at least one person injured among crashes with a known injury count—23.33% by day and 28.33% by night, where day is 06:00–19:59 and night is 20:00–05:59. This crash-level share is a defensible measure of how often a recorded crash involved injury, using all crashes with known injury counts in each period as its denominator. It leaves unanswered the risk of injury per trip or mile because traffic exposure is absent. options.reason: Fatal-crash share focuses on the most severe recorded outcome and compares it across crashes in each time period.
